passage: I'm Isha, and I was sitting two rows behind when a lab assistant told Manoj, in front of everyone, that people from his part of the country "never finish on time." Manoj went still. Dhruv shot to his feet. "I'm going straight to the head of department. Right now. I'll sort this out for you." I saw Manoj tug his sleeve, and I saw a flicker cross Manoj's face that I can't name. Dhruv stopped. He sat down, took a breath and asked, "What do you want here? Tell me and I'll back you." Manoj said quietly that he wanted to speak to the coordinator himself. On Friday they went together. Manoj talked and Dhruv stood a step behind him, saying nothing at all until Manoj looked over.

qa.q: What did the lab assistant say about people from Manoj's part of the country?
qa.a: The lab assistant said they "never finish on time."

qa.q: Why did Dhruv stop and sit down after Manoj tugged his sleeve?
qa.a: Dhruv seemed to realise he was speaking over Manoj and wanted to ask what Manoj wanted, though Isha says the reason cannot be known for sure.

qa.q: What did Dhruv do that supported Manoj's voice?
qa.a: He asked what Manoj wanted, then stood a step behind while Manoj spoke to the coordinator himself.

qa.q: How might Manoj have felt if Dhruv had gone straight to the head of department?
qa.a: Manoj might have felt helpless or sidelined, as though the situation had become Dhruv's story instead of his own.

grounding: A friend faces bias and the protagonist first wants to shield him, then asks what he wants and supports his own voice.

passage: Francis here. I noticed something odd about Samir last week when we split up our project tasks. A new teammate, Tashi, had just joined from a small hill town. Samir was about to hand Tashi the easy formatting job. Samir's pen stopped, and then Samir laughed a little awkwardly and said to me, "Wait. Why did I assume Tashi couldn't handle the data part?" It was quiet for a second. I couldn't tell whether Samir felt embarrassed or curious. What I saw was that Samir didn't argue with the thought or brush it away. Samir asked Tashi to take the data analysis. Tashi did it faster than any of us and taught the rest of us a shortcut. Samir told me afterwards, "Good to check my guesses against actual people."

qa.q: Which task was Samir about to give Tashi?
qa.a: Samir was about to hand Tashi the easy formatting job.

qa.q: What might Samir have been feeling when Samir stopped and asked "Why did I assume...?"
qa.a: Possibly awkward or curious, since Samir laughed a little awkwardly, though Francis says Francis could not tell.

qa.q: What did Samir do that worked well?
qa.a: Samir noticed the assumption without brushing it away, then tested it by asking Tashi to take the data analysis.

qa.q: How might Tashi have felt about being given the data work?
qa.a: Tashi may have felt trusted and respected, as the result was work faster than anyone else's.

grounding: The protagonist catches an assumption about a teammate's origin, notices it without shame and tests it against the real person.

passage:
Tuesday, 11.40 pm, finally home.
Okay. Deep breath. I'm still shaking a little. Coming back from the late shift, a police jeep flashed its light at me near the flyover and an officer waved me to the side. My heart was BANGING. My first thought was to walk faster. I didn't. I kept both hands where they could see them, said "Good evening," and held out my ID before they asked. "May I know why I've been stopped?" It was a routine check. The officer looked at my ID, asked where I was going, and let me go in two minutes. I had Anjali on a call the whole time with the phone in my pocket, and she stayed quiet and listened. She says I did everything right. 🙂 I'm going to sleep now.

qa.q: Where was the diary writer stopped by the police jeep?
qa.a: Near the flyover.

qa.q: What was the diary writer feeling when the officer waved to the side?
qa.a: Fear, since the heart was banging and the first urge was to walk faster.

qa.q: What helped the stop go smoothly?
qa.a: Keeping both hands visible, being polite, showing ID, asking calmly why the stop happened and having Anjali on the call.

qa.q: How might Anjali have felt listening on the phone during the stop?
qa.a: Probably anxious and helpless, but she stayed quiet so the writer could focus, and afterwards she was proud.

grounding: Stopped at night by police, the protagonist is afraid but stays calm, keeps hands visible, is polite, shows ID, asks the reason and has someone on the phone.

passage: "Sign here, and we can settle this quickly," the officer said, sliding a paper across the desk. The station smelled of old tea and dust. I'm Jyoti, and I'd only gone in after a minor scooter accident. He tapped the page, then rubbed two fingers together and said, "A small amount, and it all goes away." My palms were sweating and my mind said, just do it, just leave. But I looked at the paper and couldn't read half the words. I said, "I don't sign what I haven't understood. I'd like my brother here, or a lawyer." His face hardened. I kept my voice level and wrote down his name and badge number. Then I rang my friend Rehana, who was a law student, and she came straight over. I never signed.

qa.q: What did the officer slide across the desk?
qa.a: He slid a paper across the desk.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling as the officer pushed the paper?
qa.a: Frightened and tempted to give in, since Jyoti's palms were sweating and a voice said to just do it and leave.

qa.q: What did Jyoti do that protected Jyoti?
qa.a: Jyoti refused to sign what was not understood, asked for a brother or a lawyer, noted the name and badge number, and called Rehana.

qa.q: How might the officer have seen Jyoti's refusal?
qa.a: As an unwelcome obstacle, since his face hardened when Jyoti did not simply comply.

grounding: An officer presses for money and a signature; the protagonist refuses to sign what has not been read, asks for a family member or lawyer and notes names.

passage: Someone had lifted Yusuf's phone at the temple fair, right between the bangle stall and the balloon seller. Back in the lane, his friend Abhinav shrugged. "Don't bother, the police won't do anything." Yusuf's stomach sank. He half believed it. Still, next morning he went to the thana in a clean shirt, carrying a folder with his ID, a photo of the phone's box and the bill his uncle had kept. The constable at the desk was busy and short with him. Yusuf stayed polite and waited on the wooden bench. When his turn came he described what had happened, step by step. The constable wrote it down and gave him a stamped copy of the complaint. "Keep this," he said. "Come back if you hear anything."

qa.q: Where was Yusuf's phone stolen?
qa.a: At the temple fair, between the bangle stall and the balloon seller.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling when Abhinav said the police would do nothing?
qa.a: Doubt and worry: his stomach sank and he half believed it.

qa.q: What did Yusuf do that improved his chances of being helped?
qa.a: He brought his ID, a photo of the box and the bill, stayed polite, described events step by step and took a stamped copy of the complaint.

qa.q: How might Abhinav have seen Yusuf's trip to the police station?
qa.a: Abhinav may have expected it to be pointless, and the stamped copy might make him rethink his view.

grounding: The protagonist goes to the station to report a theft hoping for help, prepared and respectful, and leaves with a copy of the complaint.

passage: The envelope had been under the rice tin for a week. Reena knew what it was: a legal notice from a bank, about a loan her father had taken for the shop. Every time she opened the tin she felt the paper glaring at her. She hadn't slept properly and told nobody, sure it would vanish if she ignored it long enough. It didn't. On Monday she put every paper in a plastic folder, took the bus to the block office and found the legal aid clinic, where a volunteer lawyer named Yusuf asked to see everything. She said, "I don't understand any of this." Yusuf said, "Then let's take it line by line, and I'll say it in plain words." When she still frowned, he explained again, slower, with a small drawing. Her shoulders loosened.

qa.q: Where had the envelope been hidden for a week?
qa.a: It had been under the rice tin.

qa.q: Why did Reena tell nobody about the notice?
qa.a: She felt scared and lost and hoped it would vanish if she ignored it.

qa.q: What did Reena do that turned fear into a plan?
qa.a: She put every paper in a folder, went to the legal aid clinic and asked the lawyer to explain it in plain words.

qa.q: How might Yusuf see a client who says "I don't understand any of this"?
qa.a: As someone normal and worth helping, since he offered to go line by line and explained again with a drawing.

grounding: The protagonist, lost after receiving a legal notice, stops ignoring it, gathers the papers and consults a legal aid lawyer who explains in plain words.

passage: Honestly, I've told very few people about the night Eshaan rang me. I'm Chinmay. There'd been a fight outside a club near campus and the police were asking questions. Eshaan said, "Just tell them I was at your place on Saturday. Please. You're my best friend." My stomach turned over. I do love him, and for a second I nearly said yes. But I thought, if I lie to the police and it comes out, I'm in this with him. I said, "I can't say something that isn't true. But I won't leave you alone with it. Let's find a lawyer tomorrow." He was furious and hung up. The next day we sat together in a legal aid office, and he stopped being angry when the lawyer started to talk.

qa.q: What did Eshaan ask Chinmay to tell the police?
qa.a: Eshaan asked Chinmay to say he was at Chinmay's place on Saturday.

qa.q: What was Chinmay feeling when Eshaan asked for the lie?
qa.a: Torn: love for Eshaan and a near yes, but also fear of being pulled into it if the lie came out.

qa.q: What did Chinmay offer instead of lying?
qa.a: Chinmay offered to help find a lawyer, and went with Eshaan to a legal aid office the next day.

qa.q: How might Eshaan have felt when Chinmay refused?
qa.a: Hurt and furious at first, as he hung up, but calmer once a lawyer began explaining what could be done.

grounding: A friend asks the protagonist to lie to the police; the protagonist refuses a false statement but stays loyal by helping him find a lawyer.

passage: Advisor's note. Tanuja came to my office on Wednesday, still shaking. A traffic official had fined her for a parking violation at a spot with no sign, and had brushed off her questions. Her friend Zeenat came with her. Tanuja said she wanted to go back and shout at the official until they understood how unfair it was. Her fists were tight and she kept saying, "They just don't care." I let her say it all. Then we looked at what she had: Zeenat's photos of the bare wall, the receipt, the time. I helped her write a short, plain complaint to the city office, and they filed it together that afternoon. Tanuja left less furious, with something to do. I will ask her next week what reply has come.

qa.q: Who came with Tanuja to the advisor's office?
qa.a: Zeenat came with her.

qa.q: What did Tanuja want to do before the advisor helped her?
qa.a: She wanted to go back and shout at the official, feeling furious and helpless that they didn't care.

qa.q: What made the complaint stronger?
qa.a: It included Zeenat's photos of the bare wall, the receipt and the time, and it was written plainly and calmly.

qa.q: How might the official have seen the fine and Tanuja's questions?
qa.a: The official may have seen it as routine work and not as unfair, so shouting would probably have made the situation worse.

grounding: After an unfair fine the protagonist is furious and helpless; anger is turned into a calm record and a complaint instead of a confrontation.

passage:
Thursday night.
I can't stop thinking about it. While reconciling the vendor accounts today, I found invoices that don't match any delivery. Same names, bigger numbers each month. Someone senior is signing them off. My hands went cold. What if I'm wrong? What if I'm right and lose my job? Rent is due in ten days. I typed half an email to the whole management group, then deleted it. I was angry, and angry emails are the ones you can't take back. Instead I rang my cousin Charu, who works with an NGO. She said, "Keep copies somewhere safe, check the company's whistleblower policy, and let's talk to a lawyer before you tell anyone." I'm scared, but I feel a bit steadier. Tomorrow I'll copy the files at home, not at the office.

qa.q: What did the diary writer find while reconciling the vendor accounts?
qa.a: The diary writer found invoices that don't match any delivery, with the same names and bigger numbers each month.

qa.q: Why did the diary writer delete the email to the management group?
qa.a: The diary writer was angry and afraid, and knew that angry emails cannot be taken back.

qa.q: What steps did Charu suggest?
qa.a: Keep copies somewhere safe, check the company's whistleblower policy and talk to a lawyer before telling anyone.

qa.q: How might Charu see the plan to email everyone?
qa.a: Charu likely sees it as risky because it could hurt the writer before there is any protection, which is why Charu asked for a wait.

grounding: The protagonist finds evidence of fraud, fears losing everything, and chooses copies, policy and legal advice over an impulsive email.

passage:
Sunday night, can't sleep.
It's been three weeks since I reported the billing error. Since then my manager barely looks at me. Tuesday's team lunch: everyone moved their chairs a little, and the chat stopped when I sat down. Nobody has said a word about it. Feels like I'm being punished for doing the right thing. I keep thinking, was it worth it? Today I did something. I started a notes file with dates: the meeting my manager cancelled, the project I was moved off, the silence. Then I rang Sahil, who listened for an hour and reminded me that I had reported a real problem. He said integrity costs something, but it's still worth something. I'm going to book a session with the union rep tomorrow. I'm hurt, and I'm not going to stay silent about it.

qa.q: How long ago did the diary writer report the billing error?
qa.a: Three weeks ago.

qa.q: How does the diary writer feel about the reactions at work?
qa.a: Punished for doing the right thing, and hurt and doubtful about whether it was worth it.

qa.q: What did the diary writer do to protect against retaliation?
qa.a: Started a dated notes file of what changed, called Sahil for support and planned to see the union rep.

qa.q: How might the manager see the report of the billing error?
qa.a: The manager may have taken it as criticism or embarrassment, which could explain the cold shoulder, though it doesn't excuse it.

grounding: After reporting an issue the protagonist is shunned and feels punished; documenting retaliation, leaning on outside support and valuing integrity's cost.
